kurz: Why a good outcome is no proof of skill, how strongly extreme values fall back and how to evaluate your own investment record honestly.

bloecke.md:
Two portfolios have achieved the same result over ten years: 8% a year. One belongs to someone who paid the same sum into a world index every month and did nothing else. The other belongs to someone who placed four hundred orders during this time. The figures are the same; the achievements behind them are not. The figure alone does not show which of the two achievements lies behind it.

Every investment result is made up of two parts: the decisions taken and what happened afterwards. Only the sum is ever visible. The two components can never be completely separated; they can only be estimated as a range. This range is the information that is missing from the account statement.

## Continuum between skill and luck

Activities can be ranked according to how strongly luck helps determine the outcome. At one end is chess, where the stronger player almost always wins; at the other end is roulette, where skill changes nothing. Where investing lies on this axis and how many years of track record are needed as proof is calculated elsewhere. Here the focus is only on the conclusion that follows from it.

The closer an activity lies to the luck end, the less the outcome is fit to serve as a verdict on the decision. The process must then be assessed all the more strictly, because otherwise no yardstick remains. A single year on the stock market resembles a hand of poker more than a game of chess. Skill is present and has an effect, but it only becomes visible over many hands. It does not follow that skill plays no role. Nor can talent be inferred from three good years.

The greater the share of luck, the less a single outcome may count as feedback on the decision. What is assessed then is what was known at the time of the decision and how it was dealt with. What came out of it is not a yardstick for this.

## Regression to the mean

If a quantity is partly determined by chance, an extreme value is on average followed by a less extreme one. Behind this there is neither a force pulling the value back nor fatigue after success. The explanation lies in breaking the result down. A peak value arises particularly often where solid skill and favourable luck coincided. The skill component repeats itself; the luck component, by definition, does not. That is why the next value falls back on average, namely by the share that luck had contributed.

Daniel Kahneman describes how he had to explain to Israeli flight instructors why praise does no harm and reprimands do not help. The instructors had observed that a praised flight was followed by a worse one and a reprimanded flight by a better one. Both observations are correct but have nothing to do with the feedback. An exceptionally good flight is almost always followed by a more normal one. Deriving a lesson about leadership from this means telling an arithmetical effect as a story about causes. In investing, the same story goes something like this: “After the award, the manager became complacent.”

Because the luck component shrinks with the square root of the observation period, r grows with the length of the track record, but only slowly.

bloecke.md: A league table selects according to the measured result, that is, according to skill and favourable luck combined. The shorter the measurement period and the higher the dispersion, the greater the share of luck at the top. That is why winners of three-year rankings disappoint so reliably. They do not get worse, but the luck that brought them to the top does not repeat itself.

## Fund data on persistence

Of the US equity funds that were in the top quartile in 2021, none was back in the top quartile in each of the four following years up to 2025. Pure chance would give 0.25 to the power of four, that is 0.39%. The result is therefore even below the value expected by chance and is no proof of persistence. Measured within the individual categories, only around 2% of small-cap funds stayed in the top quartile throughout, and none of the large-cap, mid-cap and multi-cap funds.

For large-cap US funds, the development can be followed year by year. Of 164 funds that were in the top quartile in 2021, 20.1% were still there after one year. That is less than the 25% that would be expected under complete randomness. After two years, none were left. Over the ten years to mid-2026, around 25% of active US funds beat their passive counterpart. The measurement is strict, because a fund only counts if it survives the period and at the same time does better (Morningstar, 9,226 funds).

bloecke.md:
## Explanations after the fact

A result without an explanation is hard to bear, so one is found, for example the manager's eye for quality, the investor's discipline or an early insight into artificial intelligence. Nassim Taleb calls this the narrative fallacy. Causes are derived from random data because the story feels right. The cross-check is simple. You ask which verifiable figure supports the story. If there is none, the story merely describes the result and does not explain it.

Success stories also contain a selection error, because only those who are still around tell their story. During the Second World War, Abraham Wald had to point out that the bullet holes in the returning bombers marked the places where a hit was harmless. For funds, the same effect has been quantified. In 1996, Elton, Gruber and Blake estimated the bias caused by closed and merged funds at 0.9 percentage points a year. Every list of the “best funds of the last ten years” is therefore systematically embellished, because the failed funds do not appear in any table. In addition, memories are adjusted after the fact. Failed founders rate their original confidence lower in retrospect than it actually was. The data on this are thin, but the pattern shows up consistently.

According to Kostolany, a speculator needs four things, namely money, thoughts, patience and luck. The fourth ranks equally with the others and is the only one that cannot be trained. He also came up with a formula about patience:

bloecke.text: At the stock exchange, two times two is never four, but five minus one.

## Evaluating your own record

Most investors know their best positions but not their return. A robust evaluation takes work, but the effort is limited. It is the only feedback that is not influenced by your own story.

schritte.text: All securities accounts and all years are included, as are closed accounts and closed positions. If only the current portfolio is evaluated, survivorship bias arises in your own portfolio.

The time-weighted return measures the strategy. The money-weighted return, that is, the internal rate of return, measures your own behaviour. The difference is due solely to the timing and size of deposits and withdrawals.
The benchmark is a broad world equity index in the currency of the portfolio, set before the calculation and not changed afterwards. An index chosen after the fact can be picked to suit the result.
The comparison is based on what remains after order fees, spreads and the tax that your own strategy triggered. The gross return is not suitable for this.
Independent decisions are counted, not years. Twenty positions that all depend on the same business cycle are closer to one decision than to twenty.
Every major decision gets two grades, one for the soundness of the reasoning at the time and one for the outcome. Only the combination of both grades can be evaluated.

bloecke.md:
Two investors each start with €60,000 in equity funds for one year.

The active investor achieves 9.0% gross, that is €5,400, and realises the gain in full through sales. For equity funds, a [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] of 30% applies (Section 20 InvStG, Investment Tax Act), so €3,780 remains taxable. After the [[Saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag)|saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag)]] of €1,000 (Section 20(9) EStG, Income Tax Act), €2,780 is taxable. On this, 26.375% [[Flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)]] including solidarity surcharge is due (Section 32d(1) EStG, Section 4 SolzG 1995, Solidarity Surcharge Act), which comes to €733.23 or 1.22% of the portfolio value.

The passive investor achieves 8.0% gross and sells nothing. Only the [[Advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)|advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)]] is due (Section 18 InvStG). Base return (Basisertrag) = 60,000 × 3.20% × 0.7 = €1,344, or €940.80 after partial exemption. This is below the allowance, so the tax is €0. The base interest rate (Basiszins) of 3.20% applies to 2026; the advance lump sum is only settled in January 2027.

After taxes, 7.78% remains against 8.00%. The apparent lead of one point has disappeared without anyone having bought a wrong share. The passive investor's tax is also only deferred, and until it becomes due, the amount continues to earn a return.

## Measuring strategy and behaviour separately

Morningstar puts the gap between fund return and investor return for the decade to the end of 2025 at 1.2 percentage points a year. The funds returned 9.9%, the average dollar invested 8.7%. The gap arises solely from when and how much was bought and sold.

The figure is disputed, however. Part of the gap can arise purely arithmetically, even without anyone making a mistake. With regular contributions, more money is invested in later years, so these years count more heavily in the money-weighted return. If their returns turn out lower than those of the earlier years, the money-weighted return lags behind the time-weighted return. In the Financial Analysts Journal in 2026, Fulkerson, Jordan, Riley and Yan consider the real damage from timing to be much smaller than presented. The order of magnitude also varies. For 2025, DALBAR measures a gap of only 0.72 points for equity investors (17.16% against 17.88%), but 2.41% against 7.30% for bond investors. What is undisputed is the method of calculating both returns. This lets you see separately what is due to the strategy and what is due to your own entries and exits.

bloecke.titel: Process and outcome as two axes
bloecke.unter: Process and outcome only match on the diagonal; the two other fields lead to false lessons.

felder.text: The reasoning was sound, the position size justifiable, the market went the other way. Nothing to change; readjusting does harm here.
Good reasoning, good outcome. One of the two fields from which the process may be adopted unchanged.
Thin reasoning, bad outcome. Unpleasant but instructive. The feedback points in the right direction.
Thin reasoning, good outcome. It rewards behaviour that will be expensive next time, and it feels like confirmation.

bloecke.md: The field at the bottom right explains why experience on the stock exchange becomes useful so slowly. With quick and unambiguous feedback, as in chess or anaesthesia, intuition develops reliably. With slow feedback overlaid by chance, a false intuition develops just as reliably. Record-keeping is enough to correct this; strength of character is not required. You record the reasoning before the outcome so that you can later read what you thought at the time instead of trusting your memory.

Once a year, on a fixed date, you gather the portfolio statements of all accounts, calculate the time-weighted and the money-weighted return and compare them, after costs and taxes, with the index set in advance. You then write down the three biggest decisions of the year, each with the reasoning at the time, the outcome and its classification in one of the four fields. If, after three years, there are more entries at the bottom right than at the top right, the gains come from a lucky streak and not from your own judgement.

Record-keeping serves accuracy; humility is not its purpose. If you know that a large part of your own result consists of luck, two practical conclusions follow. First, you choose position sizes so that a run of bad luck does not threaten your livelihood. Second, you do not read your success rate as permission to take more risk next time. Both are cheaper than the alternative of mistaking a random streak for an ability until the market shows that it was not one.

mitnehmen: Every result is made up of decision and luck; only the sum is visible, and the components can only be separated as a range.
Regression to the mean follows from the fact that the luck component of an extreme value does not repeat itself.
Rankings select by outcome and therefore systematically favour candidates who had good luck, which is why short-term winners disappoint so reliably.
An honest self-assessment needs all accounts, both types of return, an index set in advance and the taxes that your own strategy triggered.
Most dangerous is a gain after poor reasoning, because it rewards the wrong behaviour.

begriffe.text: Statistical consequence of the fact that an extreme value usually consists of skill and favourable luck. The luck component does not repeat itself, so the next value falls back on average. The effect is purely arithmetical and is not based on any force.

Share of an observed lead that repeats itself on average. It corresponds to the share of skill in the total observed dispersion and grows with the length of the observation period, because the dispersion due to luck shrinks with the square root of the duration.
Tendency to derive causal stories from random data because an explanation feels more right than chance. A remedy is to ask which verifiable figure supports the story.
Return that strips out deposits and withdrawals and thus measures the strategy or the fund, regardless of when money flowed in.

Internal rate of return of the portfolio. It weights each period by the capital invested at the time and thus measures your own entries and exits. The difference from the time-weighted return is due solely to the timing and size of deposits and withdrawals.
